overview: Dilophosaurus was a large Early Jurassic theropod from Arizona, about six metres long, bearing two thin parallel bony crests along the skull roof. These were display structures — far too fragile for combat — and Dilophosaurus was one of the largest terrestrial predators of its time at ~193 million years ago.

The Jurassic Park portrayal of Dilophosaurus with an expandable neck frill and venom is entirely fictional; no fossil evidence supports either feature. The notch in its upper jaw between the premaxilla and maxilla once led to scavenging hypotheses, since largely refuted by biomechanical analysis.

fossilSites.name: Kayenta Formation
fossilSites.note: Lower Jurassic continental deposits with the type specimen and additional material alongside prosauropods and tritylodontid cynodonts.

articles.title: Discovery and naming
articles.body: Sam Welles first described material from the Kayenta Formation in 1954, initially identifying it as a large Megalosaurus. He renamed it Dilophosaurus wetherilli in 1970, honouring Navajo guide Jesse Wetherbee. A second specimen found in 1964 provided much of the postcranial anatomy known today.

articles.title: Skull crests
articles.body: The twin crests run from the snout to above the orbits, formed by the nasal bones. Their paper-thin construction rules out a weapon function. Analogous thin cranial crests in other theropods (Oviraptor, Guanlong) and in cassowaries are consistently associated with display and species recognition.

articles.title: Ecology
articles.body: Dilophosaurus represents a transitional grade between small coelophysoids and the larger tetanurans that dominated the Jurassic. In the Kayenta Formation it coexisted with the prosauropod Massospondylus and early crocodylomorphs in a seasonally arid environment, probably pursuing medium-sized prey.

record.description: Dilophosaurus wetherilli was a large early theropod from the Kayenta Formation of Arizona. Several partial skeletons, including substantial skull material, document paired cranial crests and a powerful bipedal predator very unlike its fictionalised venom-spitting portrayal.
facts: There is no fossil evidence for venom glands or an expandable neck frill.
The paired crests were thin and probably visual structures, though their exact function is unknown.
Modern re-preparation shows a more robust skull and skeleton than older weak-jawed reconstructions.

presentation.heroLead: A large, twin-crested predator from the Early Jurassic of Arizona, known from several partial skeletons that make it one of the best-documented early theropods.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Dilophosaurus wetherilli
heroMedia.alt: Scientific life restoration of Dilophosaurus wetherilli walking in side view, showing the paired skull crests
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration based on the 2020 anatomical revision by Marsh and Rowe. Skin texture, colour and the soft-tissue outline of the crests are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Dilophosaurus was a long-bodied, lightly built predator about six to seven metres long, with a long neck, a low skull carrying a pair of thin bony crests, and hands with four fingers. It is the largest land animal known from the Kayenta Formation and among the largest theropods of the Early Jurassic anywhere.

Older reconstructions showed a weak-jawed animal with a notch beneath the nostrils, sometimes interpreted as a sign of scavenging. Re-preparation of the type material and study of a fourth skeleton showed that the jaws and skull were more robust than once thought, and that the crests were supported by extensions of the nasal and lacrimal bones and hollowed out by air spaces linked to the sinuses.

The animal in the Jurassic Park films bears its name but little else. There is no fossil evidence for venom, a neck frill or a small body; the real Dilophosaurus was a substantial hunter whose crests were probably visual structures, though their exact function cannot be tested from bones alone.
animalHighlights: Two thin, plate-like crests rose from the top of the snout, formed by the nasal and lacrimal bones and pierced by air spaces.
A long neck, slender tail and four-fingered hands place Dilophosaurus among early neotheropods rather than later, more compact predators.
The holotype skeleton preserves healed injuries on several bones, showing that the animal survived serious damage during life.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Blade-like, serrated teeth and a large gape indicate a predator, but no gut contents or bite marks tie it to particular prey.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long hindlimbs and short forelimbs show habitual two-legged walking. Tracks from the region have been linked to similar theropods, but none can be assigned to Dilophosaurus with certainty.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is reconstructed from incomplete individuals; mass estimates of a few hundred kilograms depend on modelling rather than direct measurement.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The crests, skull shape and proportions are known from bone; colour, skin covering and any soft extension of the crests are not preserved.

locality.name: Kayenta Formation exposures near Tuba City
locality.note: The type specimens were found in 1942 on Navajo land west of Tuba City. The map point is a regional reference rather than the exact quarry.

presentation.classificationSummary: Dilophosaurus is an early neotheropod. It was long grouped with Coelophysis and its relatives, but the 2020 revision by Marsh and Rowe recovered it closer to the later, larger theropods of the Middle and Late Jurassic. Its exact position remains sensitive to analysis.

questions.title: What were the crests for?
questions.copy: They were thin and probably served for display or recognition, but no fossil evidence tests these ideas directly and any soft-tissue extension is unknown.

questions.title: Where does it sit among early theropods?
questions.copy: Analyses disagree on whether Dilophosaurus is close to Coelophysis or nearer the ancestry of later large theropods. The 2020 revision favours the latter.

questions.title: How much of the skull is original?
questions.copy: The holotype skull was partly reconstructed in plaster for decades. Modern re-preparation separated bone from restoration, but some regions remain distorted.

review.ageReviewNote: U-Pb dating places the fossil-bearing Kayenta interval near 193 Ma in the Sinemurian.

panel.headline: Several partial skeletons with skull material from one Arizona rock unit.
panel.standfirst: Dilophosaurus is known from a small number of partial skeletons collected from the Kayenta Formation of northern Arizona since 1942, including the holotype and a second skeleton found together. The 2020 revision re-described all of the material and added a further specimen.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions are represented across a handful of individuals, including substantial skull material, but no single skeleton is complete and several bones are crushed or distorted.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype preserves much of the skull and lower jaw together with most of the vertebral column, girdles and limbs. A second skeleton found beside it, a larger crested individual collected in 1964, and a fourth skeleton in the Texas collections add overlapping cranial and postcranial material.
knownRemains.note: Different specimens are complete in different regions, so the composite skeleton is well understood even though every individual has gaps. Earlier restoration in plaster complicated study of the type skull.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Much of the skull and both lower jaws in the holotype, including the crest-bearing nasals and lacrimals; further skull material in referred specimens.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae with ribs and chevrons across several individuals; the tail is incompletely known.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Shoulder and hip girdles, forelimbs with four-fingered hands, hindlimbs and feet, represented across specimens.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Healed fractures and other pathologies on the holotype; no skin, feathers, colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: UCMP 37302 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull and much of the skeleton found by Jesse Williams and collected by Samuel Welles in 1942. First named Megalosaurus wetherilli in 1954 and renamed Dilophosaurus in 1970 once the crests were recognised.
specimenCards.meta: Near Tuba City, Arizona · Kayenta Formation · University of California Museum of Paleontology

specimenCards.title: UCMP 37303, UCMP 77270 and TMM 43646-1
specimenCards.description: A second, more fragmentary skeleton found beside the holotype, a larger crested individual collected in 1964, and a further skeleton in the Texas Vertebrate Paleontology Collections described in the 2020 revision.
specimenCards.meta: Kayenta Formation · Arizona · University of California and University of Texas collections

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Paired thin skull crests, serrated teeth, a long neck and four-fingered hands preserved in bone from several individuals, plus healed injuries on the holotype.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A large bipedal predator whose crests were probably visual structures; its relationships lie among early neotheropods, with the 2020 revision placing it closer to later large theropods than to Coelophysis.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Crest function, colour and skin, the exact form of the tail tip, and whether isolated tracks and other Kayenta fragments belong to the genus.
